strengths: Addresses an important and hard problem (nonparametric CI testing) with a principled framing via the partial covariance operator, and connects it to modern spectral/contrastive representation learning—an appealing and timely direction.

The proposed test statistic has a tractable chi-squared null distribution, which is a genuine practical advantage over permutation/resampling-based CI tests that must estimate p-values empirically and scale poorly.

The bi-level contrastive algorithm (Algorithm 1) is a concrete and reasonable extension of Kostic et al. (2024) to the conditional/partial-covariance setting, with an explicit whitening post-processing step.

The paper is honest that the experiments are preliminary and that the no-free-lunch theorem (Shah & Peters, 2020) limits uniform guarantees, and it frames validity relative to representation quality rather than claiming uniform validity.
weaknesses: The central validity claim (Thm. 4.1) is conditional on an unproven assumption that representation learning is consistent (E_m -> 0). This is not established anywhere, and it is essentially the same representation-consistency requirement the paper criticizes in regression-based tests (Shah & Peters; Pogodin et al.). Moreover, under H0 the target operator Sigma_{X Y.Z} is identically zero, so the meaning of 'learning the leading spectral features' (and hence E_m -> 0) is ill-defined under the null, which the paper does not address.

The chi-squared null distribution requires the population partial covariance of the learned features to vanish under H0. This holds only if the conditional means E[u(X)|Z] and E[v(Y)|Z] lie in the linear span of w(Z). A simple example (Z~N(0,1), X=Z+eps_X, Y=Z+eps_Y, w(Z)=Z^2) gives a non-zero partial covariance under H0, so the test is not valid for arbitrary features. The proof (App. B.5-B.8) applies a Lindeberg-Feller CLT to essentially uncentered summands, which implicitly presumes a zero population mean; this gap is not made explicit.

Equation (3), the definition of the partial cross-covariance operator, is garbled/incorrect (Sigma_AB - Sigma_AC Sigma_CB.), missing the inverse of the (partial) covariance operator. This is a foundational definition on which the entire method rests.

The claim 'A ⟂ B | C iff ||Sigma_{A(B,C).C}|| = 0' is stated without the necessary conditions (invertibility of the relevant covariance operator / characteristic-feature or conditional-mean-embedding conditions) that are required in the L^2 setting. The characterization is cited to Strobl et al. (2019) but not justified, and it is central to the paper's premise.

The power result (Thm. 4.2) has internal inconsistencies: the statement requires eps_n^2 >= 2d E_m^2 + ... while the proof derives d E_m^2 (and elsewhere d E_m). There is also no practical guidance on choosing d, even though d enters both the signal-capture condition and all error terms.

The experimental evidence is far too preliminary and is inconsistent with the description: the text says 8 competing methods are compared and d_Z ranges from 100-500, but the figures show only 3 methods (Ours/KCI/GCIT) and d_Z from 10-250; the figures appear to be low-resolution placeholders, and leftover 'low prio' annotations remain. Critically, no runtime/scalability experiments are reported despite 'scalable' being a headline claim.

Presentation problems undermine confidence: inconsistent naming (SCIT in the abstract/figure vs SpecCIT in the experiments), typos ('crain', 'computing', 'for for t=1...'), and a mismatch between the claimed 'comprehensive theoretical analysis' and the acknowledged 'preliminary experiments.'

The novelty is incremental: the core spectral contrastive machinery is from Kostic et al. (2024), and the theory largely composes standard tools (CLT, covariance concentration). The claimed advantage over regression-based CI tests ('simpler' validity requirements) is asserted but not demonstrated.

strengths: The research direction is sensible and novel: recasting nonparametric conditional independence (CI) testing through the partial covariance operator and applying learned spectral features bridges kernel-based theory with modern contrastive representation learning. This is a legitimate and underexplored angle.

The technical extension is non-trivial: handling the composition of covariance operators in the partial covariance operator via a rank-2d auxiliary (bi-level) problem, and connecting it to a contrastive loss reminiscent of Kostic et al. (2024), is a genuine methodological contribution rather than a trivial adaptation.

The theoretical ambition is high: the paper attempts a complete asymptotic treatment, characterizing the null distribution of the test statistic as chi-squared and providing a power guarantee under local alternatives.
weaknesses: The central validity claim is conditional on an unproven assumption. Theorem 4.1 and 4.2 require the representation-learning error to satisfy E_m -> 0 (with sqrt(d) E_m -> 0 for the power result), but the paper never establishes when Algorithm 1 actually achieves this. There is no convergence proof for the learned features to the true spectral functions, so the guarantees are essentially assumed rather than derived; the method's value hinges entirely on an empirically unvalidated condition (E_m is never measured in experiments).

The experiments are far too thin and contain internal inconsistencies. Only a single synthetic benchmark (the post-nonlinear model) is used, with no real-world data despite the motivating cancer-genetics example. The text claims eight baselines (KCIT, RCIT, Scetbon, GCIT, DGCIT, CDCIT, NNLSCIT, CCIT), yet Figures 2 and 3 display only three methods (Ours, KCI, GCIT); the text states d_Z is varied from 100 to 500 while the figures show dim_z from 10 to 250. This undermines both the evidential support and reproducibility.

There is a mismatch between the headline claim and the evidence. The title promises 'Scalable' testing, but no runtime, memory, or scaling study is provided, and the largest reported conditioning dimension is small. The paper also repeatedly self-describes its results as 'preliminary' (abstract, contributions, conclusion), which is inappropriate for a top-tier submission and signals that the work is not ready.

Inconsistency between the main text and the appendix. The power condition in Theorem 4.2 (main text) is stated as epsilon_n^2 >= 2d E_m^2 + c(d^2 + log delta^-1)/n, whereas the appendix proof derives epsilon_n^2 > d E_m^2 + [C^2K^2(d^2 + d log delta^-1) + c_alpha]/n with different constants. The relationship between the training size m and test size n is also never made precise.

Presentation quality is poor. There are leftover editorial notes ('Scetbon (low prio)', 'CDCIT (low prio)'), typos ('crain' for 'train'), garbled loss subscripts, broken reference labels/years, and an apparently truncated definition of the partial covariance operator in Eq. (3) (Sigma_{AB.C} = Sigma_{AB} - Sigma_{AC} Sigma_{CB.}).

Reproducibility is inadequate. Figures appear to be low-resolution placeholders, and there is no information on network architectures, hyperparameters, optimization settings, d-selection, or released code.

Key practical questions are unaddressed: how d should be chosen in practice, the computational cost of the bi-level optimization, and how the framework escapes the Shah & Peters no-free-lunch barrier in a way that yields useful power in realistic settings (the abstract acknowledges the barrier but the reconciliation is left informal).

strengths: The core idea is novel and principled: recasting nonparametric CI testing through the Hilbert–Schmidt norm of the partial covariance operator and replacing fixed kernels with learned spectral features is a fresh and well-motivated direction that bridges kernel CI theory and modern representation learning.

The bi-level contrastive formulation (Section 3, Appendix A) is a genuine technical advance: extending the spectral representation learning of Kostic et al. (2024) to the partial/conditional case is nontrivial because the composition term $\Sigma_{XZ}\Sigma_{Z\hat{Y}}$ does not admit an unbiased empirical estimator, and the auxiliary rank-2d projection W is a clever workaround.

The theoretical results are useful even if conditional: characterizing the null distribution as asymptotically $\chi^2(d^2)$ (Thm 4.1) and giving a non-asymptotic power guarantee (Thm 4.2) links representation-learning error $\mathcal{E}_m$ to test validity/power, which is a cleaner condition than the uniform conditional-mean-embedding rates required by regression-based tests.

The problem is important and the paper is honest about the hardness (Shah & Peters no-free-lunch) and about framing validity/power through representation quality rather than claiming universal validity.
weaknesses: The central validity claim is conditional on an assumption that is essentially the crux of the problem. Theorem 4.1 requires $\mathcal{E}_m \to 0$ (consistent learning of the leading spectral features), but no convergence guarantee is provided for Algorithm 1. The paper therefore establishes 'if we could learn the true spectral features, the test is valid'—assuming away the hardest part. Likewise the $\chi^2(d^2)$ limit depends on whitening making $\mathrm{Cov}(u_\theta(x))\otimes\mathrm{Cov}(v_\theta(\bar y))\approx I$, which again presupposes near-perfect learning.

The empirical evaluation is preliminary and internally inconsistent, so it does not support the headline claims. The text states $d_Z$ ranges from 100 to 500 and lists eight baselines (KCIT, RCIT, Scetbon, GCIT, DGCIT, CDCIT, NNLSCIT, CCIT), but the figures show $d_Z$ from 10 to 250 and only three methods (Ours, KCI, GCIT). The power figure shows all methods at power 1.0 across all dimensions, which is non-discriminative and does not substantiate any advantage.

The 'scalable' claim is not demonstrated. There is no runtime/memory comparison against kernel or permutation baselines, no scaling study, and no experiment in the regime where kernel methods are known to fail; scalability is asserted rather than measured.

Several presentation and correctness issues: typos ('Frobenious', 'crain'), naming inconsistency (SCIT in Fig. 1 vs SpecCIT in text), an incomplete/ambiguous partial covariance formula in Eq. (3) (the $\Sigma_{CC}^{-1}$/whitening convention is not stated), mismatched bracketed years in the reference list, and inconsistencies between Theorem 4.2 and its proof in B.9 (the signal condition appears as $d\,\mathcal{E}_m$ in one place and $d\,\mathcal{E}_m^2$ in another).

The contribution is somewhat incremental relative to Kostic et al. (2024): the spectral-learning machinery is imported largely intact, and the novel element is its application to CI testing plus the conditional extension. There is no explicit limitations section, and the sub-Gaussianity and exact-whitening assumptions are strong and unexamined for realistic neural features.

strengths: Novel integration of spectral representation learning with partial covariance operators for conditional independence testing, extending recent contrastive spectral methods to a new inference task.
The bi-level contrastive algorithm is a creative technical contribution that addresses the unobservable residualization with respect to Z by learning auxiliary features W.

Experiments on synthetic and real data suggest potential practical advantages: robustness to nonsmooth alternatives, scalability relative to kernel methods, and the ability to detect nonlinear dependencies in a breast cancer application.
The paper includes a limitations section that honestly discusses the lack of standardized hyperparameter protocols and the dependence of guarantees on representation quality.
weaknesses: The proof of the main validity result (Theorem 4.1) is invalid. In the covariance calculation around Eq. (26), the authors incorrectly assume E[u(x)u(x)^T ⊗ v(y)v(y)^T] = E[u(x)u(x)^T] ⊗ E[v(y)v(y)^T] under the null. This equality would require unconditional independence of u(x) and v(y), but the null only gives conditional independence given Z. Because both features can depend on Z, the covariance is generally not I_{d^2}, and the claimed χ²(d²) null distribution does not follow.

The off-diagonal terms in the decomposition of the test statistic are claimed to be negligible (Lemma B.3 and Appendix B.7), but this is false. For simple linear Gaussian examples, the off-diagonal contribution is of the same order as the diagonal term and is essential for residualizing Z. The mean calculation for the off-diagonal term incorrectly treats Q_{ij} as independent of u(x_i) and v(y_j). Consequently, the approximation T_n ≈ n||Û^T Q V̂||_F² and the subsequent CLT argument are not justified.

The validity guarantee relies only on the whitening error E_m^val → 0. Under the null, the partial covariance operator is zero, so the inner problem for W is unconstrained and W need not span the conditional mean functions of U and V given Z. Without an additional error term controlling how well W residualizes Z, the null distribution of the test statistic depends on the unknown conditional dependence structure and is not distribution-free.

The power analysis (Theorem 4.2 and Appendix B.9) inherits the flawed validity framework and contains notational confusion. The error term E_m^pow is not clearly linked to the approximation of the partial covariance matrix, and no explicit non-asymptotic rates are provided for the learned representations.

The experimental evaluation is not sufficient to compensate for the theoretical gaps. No code is released, there is no standardized CI benchmark, and the real-data experiment lacks ground truth for conditional independence. The breast cancer conclusion is based on p-values from one method and a predictive accuracy comparison that may reflect overfitting rather than a true conditional dependence.

The dimension pruning step used at test time is a heuristic that changes the degrees of freedom of the reference χ² distribution. It is not covered by the theory and could affect Type I error control, yet no calibration study is provided for the pruned statistic.

Presentation issues reduce clarity and reproducibility: several typos and notational inconsistencies (e.g., Algorithm 1 updates only wθ, uθ, vθ while the losses also contain learnable Mθ and Nθ; Eq. (10) is reused with different meanings in the main text and appendix; figure references and captions are sometimes mismatched).

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem (scalable/valid conditional independence testing) with clear relevance to causal discovery, feature selection, and computational pathology; the introduction and motivation are strong.

Proposes a genuinely novel technical construction: a bi-level contrastive algorithm that extends spectral representation learning of covariance operators to the *partial* covariance operator by introducing a low-rank auxiliary (inner) problem for the Z-residualization, which is non-trivial relative to prior spectral-learning work (Kostic et al. 2024; Sun et al. 2025).

Provides a theoretical analysis with explicit dependence on representation quality (the E_m^val and E_m^pow terms), characterizing an asymptotic chi-squared null and a power threshold, rather than relying on the restrictive smoothness/regression-rate assumptions of competing tests.

Broad empirical evaluation: synthetic post-nonlinear benchmarks, a nonsmooth high-dimensional setting that breaks local-permutation assumptions, a novel high-dimensional benchmark, hyperparameter-sensitivity ablations, runtime comparisons, a Sachs-inspired CI-query study, and a real TCGA-BRCA application.
Honest limitations section that explicitly flags the open problem of non-asymptotic rates for learned spectral representations and the lack of a standard hyperparameter-tuning protocol for CI tests.
weaknesses: The central validity and power guarantees are conditional on the representation-learning error vanishing (E_m^val, E_m^pow -> 0). This is not established and is acknowledged by the authors as an open problem. Consequently, the end-to-end validity of SpectralCIT is not actually proven; the hardest part of the pipeline (learning representations with controlled error) is assumed away. The theorems therefore largely assert 'if the features are good, the test works.'

Under the null the partial covariance operator is identically zero, so the leading singular functions are not identified and the spectral representation learning problem is degenerate/ill-posed. The paper does not analyze what the algorithm learns under H0, nor whether the required orthonormality/covariance structure holds on the held-out test set in this regime. Since validity is precisely the property that must hold under H0, this is a serious gap in the soundness of the core claim.

The real-data evidence is weak: the breast-cancer conclusion rests on a single CI test on a single dataset, where a rejection (p < 10^-3) cannot be distinguished from a type I error. The XGBoost 'confirmation' is circular — showing X adds predictive signal does not validate the CI test. Given that the method is described as conservative in synthetic settings, the strong rejection here is not well-justified as a true positive.

The test-time rank selection (SVD of the test statistic, retaining leading triplets, then correcting the chi-squared degrees of freedom) is data-dependent. Selecting the largest singular values biases the statistic upward, and there is no theoretical justification that the post-hoc adjusted chi-squared approximation remains valid. This threatens the very type I error control the paper claims to establish.

Empirical advantages over the strongest baseline (NNLSCT) are modest: NNLSCT is competitive in the post-nonlinear benchmark and the advantage is confined mainly to the nonsmooth setting and runtime. The scalability claim ('~2x faster than KCIT') is thin, and more scalable recent methods (e.g., Pogodin et al. 2025, cited in related work) are not compared despite being directly relevant to the scalability claim.

Minor reproducibility/presentation issues: no code or data link is provided for a fairly complex bi-level optimization; there are apparent numerical inconsistencies (the high-dimensional benchmark is described as 500 repetitions in the text but '5 times' in the figure caption), and there is potential tension between the text asserting NNLSCT maintains type I error control and the type-I-error trends in the figures that should be reconciled.

The theoretical setup also assumes a spectral gap (sigma_d > sigma_{d+1}) and a local-alternative separation epsilon_n that decays with n; the practical regime in which these hold (and how d should be chosen to satisfy them) is not connected to the experiments.

strengths: Original and timely idea: extending spectral representation learning for statistical operators to conditional independence testing via a bi-level contrastive algorithm for partial covariance operators is novel and connects kernel CI theory with modern representation learning.

The proposed SpectralCIT test is simple and computationally appealing: it reduces testing to a low-rank matrix statistic n||C_UV - C_UW C_WV||_F^2 and uses a chi-square critical value, which is easy to implement and potentially more scalable than kernel matrix methods.

The empirical evaluation is broad and includes challenging synthetic settings (post-nonlinear, nonsmooth, high-dimensional) and a real TCGA-BRCA case study; in several settings SpectralCIT controls Type I error while maintaining competitive power.
The paper includes useful practical details (hyperparameter grids, sensitivity analysis, runtime comparisons, pruning, whitening) and an honest limitations section.
weaknesses: The central validity claim (Theorem 4.1) is not adequately supported. The proof assumes E[(u(X)⊗v(Y,Z))(u(X)⊗v(Y,Z))^T] = Cov(u)⊗Cov(v) under H0, but conditional independence given Z does not imply unconditional independence of u(X) and v(Y,Z), especially since v is a function of Z as well. Thus the limiting covariance of the test statistic is not generally the identity, and the χ²(d²) null distribution does not follow from the argument as stated.

Even at the population level, the finite-dimensional W need not span the conditional mean functions E[u(X)|Z] and E[v(Y,Z)|Z], so C_UV - C_UW C_WV need not vanish under H0. The theory does not impose or verify a sufficiency condition on the learned W, leaving a major gap between the null hypothesis and the test statistic.

The definition of the partial covariance operator in Eq. (3), Σ_AB·C = Σ_AB - Σ_AC Σ_CB, is missing the inverse/regularization term Σ_CC^{-1} unless Σ_CC is identity. This is either a notational error or an unstated assumption, and it makes the background mathematically imprecise.

The real-data experiment violates the i.i.d. assumption used in the theory: up to 10 patches are taken per WSI, yielding 1341 triplets that are not independent. This can invalidate the reported p-values and may explain why SpectralCIT rejects the null while KCIT and NNLSCIT do not.

The power guarantee (Theorem 4.2) relies on an abstract representation-error term and an unspecified choice of d, while the test-time dimension pruning is data-dependent and not covered by the theory. It is therefore unclear how to choose d in practice to satisfy the theorem.

Scalability is only partially demonstrated: experiments use N=1000 and d_Z≤300, with runtime about 2× faster than KCIT but slower than RCIT. The claim of addressing scalability limitations is not fully supported by large-scale benchmarks.

Baseline tuning is not fully equalized: NNLSCIT uses hyperparameters from the original paper, while SpectralCIT, RCIT, GCIT, and DGCIT are tuned with 30 Bayesian trials; this may favor the proposed method. No code release or reproducibility artifact is mentioned.
The paper contains several presentation issues (e.g., 'NNLSCT' vs 'NNLSCIT', missing letters, dense proof exposition) and some references to 2026 work, which make the manuscript harder to verify.
